sections.h2: Who does what on property tax in Camden County?
sections.html:
Three layers share the work in Camden County. The municipal assessor sets the value of each parcel, the municipal tax collector sends the bill and takes payment, and the Camden County Board of Taxation hears assessment appeals. The board sits at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, has public hours on weekdays from 9 to 4 and a phone line at 856-225-5238.

A single bill covers several taxing bodies. In Cherry Hill, the county's most populous town, the township's own 2026 breakdown shows the county levy at 18.86 percent of an average bill, with the school district taking the biggest share. Owners in the other towns see a different mix, so the back of your bill is the place to check your own split.

  • Name or mailing address changes go through the municipal assessor's office, in writing.
  • Questions about how much you owe or when it is due go to your town's tax collector.
  • A value you think is too high becomes a case for the county board, once you have spoken with your assessor.

sections.h2: What is Camden County like beyond the tax bill?
sections.html:
Camden County covers 221.36 square miles of land along the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia, and its ground is flat and low. Its highest surveyed point is about 219 feet above sea level. The county seat is the city of Camden, incorporated in 1828, and the county is split into 36 municipalities, from dense river towns to the wooded suburbs near Voorhees and Cherry Hill.

For July 2025 the Census Bureau counts 535,799 residents, compared with 523,500 in April 2020. Typical home value runs about $287,100, about 64.7 percent of households own, and the middle household earns $88,755 a year. The home value sits well below the $524,100 median in Essex County, so price a Camden County house against nearby local sales.

  • Employers include Campbell's and Subaru of America, both headquartered in the county, plus medical schools run with Rowan University in Camden and Stratford.
  • The PATCO Speedline runs from Philadelphia through Camden to Lindenwold, with stops at Woodcrest, Westmont and Collingswood.
  • Low, flat ground and an aging storm drain system leave parts of the county exposed to flooding, which buyers and inspectors look at closely.

sections.h2: When can you appeal a Camden County assessment?
sections.html:
You can file with the county board from the time assessment notices go out until the 4 p.m. close on April 1, or the 45th day after the town finishes its notice mailing, whichever is later. The paper has to physically reach the board by then. A postmark does not count, and a late petition is dismissed.

Towns that have just finished a revaluation or reassessment get a one-month extension to May 1. The board's website names the towns in that position for the current cycle, and a deadline falling on a Sunday or legal holiday slides to the following working day. Bills for added or omitted assessments, which come from new construction or an error on the tax list, follow their own December 1 rule.

Camden County Board of Taxation filing rules, per the board's own instructions
SituationRule
Regular appealIn the board's hands by the 4 p.m. close on April 1, or 45 days after notices are mailed if that is later
Town revalued or reassessedIn hand by the 4 p.m. close on May 1
Added or omitted assessmentIn hand by December 1, or a month after the collector mails those bills if that is later
Comparable sales evidenceAt the board, assessor and clerk at least 7 days before the hearing
Further appealTax Court of New Jersey, filed inside 45 days of the judgment

sections.h2: How do you file an appeal with the Camden County board?
sections.html:
The board accepts petitions online, by mail and in person, and it holds hearings in a virtual format as well as at its Blackwood location. Online filing runs through a site the board names on its appeals page, which works best in Chrome, Safari or Firefox. The paper form is on the board's forms page.

  • File one petition per parcel, with the filing fee attached: $5 under $150,000 of assessed value, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1,000,000, and $150 above that.
  • Send a copy to the assessor and the clerk of your town.
  • Use up to five comparable sales, with block, lot, sale price and deed date. Comparable assessments do not count as evidence.
  • Pay your quarterly installments while the case is open, at least through the first quarter, unless the board relaxes that rule.

The appeal covers the assessed value alone, and the number the board wants proven is market value as of October 1 of the year before the tax year. If the board lowers your value, the judgment is held in place for that year and the next two unless something such as a town revaluation changes it.

sections.h2: Can a Camden County house sell while tax is still owed?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax stays attached to the house, so the balance has to be dealt with by the closing table. New Jersey towns charge 8 percent interest on the first $1,500 of a delinquency and 18 percent above that, counted back to the due date once the grace period passes. Cherry Hill, for example, gives a 10-day grace period and refuses postmarks.

If a town sells a tax lien on your property, the house cannot be sold until the lien is redeemed. A buyer who holds the lien can start foreclosure in state court if it stays open for two years. Before signing a sale contract, ask your town collector for a payoff in writing, with interest calculated to a named day.

  • Pass the latest bill to the buyer or title company.
  • Check sewer and water accounts separately, because many towns bill them apart from the tax.
  • Several quarters behind? Ask for the payoff early so the closing agent has time to plan.

sections.h2: Which tax relief programs reach Camden County homeowners?
sections.html:
The state's fiscal year 2027 budget funds three relief programs for owners and renters: Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. The filing deadline for the 2025 application was November 2, 2026, so that window has closed, and the Division of Taxation's relief page is where the next application window is posted.

Locally, the municipal assessor takes the state-mandated deductions: $250 for qualifying veterans, $250 for seniors and disabled owners who meet the income limit, and a full exemption for owners with a 100 percent permanent and total service-connected disability. Each has residency and ownership tests dated October 1 of the year before the tax year. Ask your town assessor for the current application.

faqs.q: Which office takes a Camden County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: The board at 509 Lakeland Road, Blackwood, NJ 08012, accepts petitions online, by mail or at the counter. Call 856-225-5238 with questions, and give your town assessor and clerk a copy.

faqs.q: Does the April 1 appeal date ever change?
faqs.a: Yes. Towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment use May 1 instead. In every case the petition has to be in the board's hands by 4:00 p.m. on the last day.

faqs.q: Does an appeal lower my tax bill right away?
faqs.a: No. You keep paying your installments, at least through the first quarter, while the case is pending. A reduction in value carries into later bills and any overpayment is dealt with after judgment.

faqs.q: Can I sell with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Tax, interest and any lien are settled from the money the seller receives at closing. A written payoff from your town collector should be in hand before you pick a closing date.

faqs.q: Who sets Camden County tax rates?
faqs.a: Each town's rate comes from the combined school, municipal, county and any special district levies divided by the town's total assessed value. The county board of taxation sets the rate, and your municipal collector bills it.
